references.text: The same chapter describes the anointing oil as also to be made by a perfumer (רוֹקֵחַ), showing the same craft technique for holy preparations.
The preceding verse lists the ingredients for the incense that is to be blended into the holy incense mentioned in verse 35.
This verse emphasizes that the incense is holy (קֹדֶשׁ) to the Lord and must not be made for personal use.
Salt (מֶלַח) was to be added to all grain offerings, reflecting the requirement that the incense should be salted (מְמֻלָּח).
Pure (טָהוֹר) frankincense was placed on the bread of the Presence, illustrating the use of pure ingredients in tabernacle service.
The priests were responsible for blending the anointing oil, connecting to the perfumer's craft mentioned in Exodus.
The Levites were responsible for the incense and the holy objects in the temple.
Ecclesiastes compares a good name to precious ointment, highlighting the value of the perfumer's art.
The verse confirms that the incense was made according to the same strict perfumer standard as the oil, emphasizing the unity of the sanctuary furnishings.
The verse affirms the theological unity between the oil and the incense, both requiring a divine recipe to be holy.
